sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Vantaa has just ended its free first hour of street parking, the last such rule among large Finnish cities. On 16 April 2026 Yle reported that the urban space committee had voted 8 to 7 to abolish it, with the city estimating that on-street parking income would rise from about 250,000 euros to 850,000 euros in 2027, since 70 to 80 percent of users of paid spaces had paid nothing [0]. On 25 September 2026 the city announced that the free hour in Tikkurila, Myyrmäki, Kivistö and Kuusijärvi would end at the start of October once signs are updated, that Saturday paid hours in Tikkurila and Myyrmäki would extend from 9-15 to 9-17, and that rates stay at 2 euros an hour in central Tikkurila and 1 euro in the second zone [1]. Park-and-ride parking without a public transport ticket rises to 7 euros for 16 hours from 5 euros [2]. The city's parking page, read in October 2026, states that most parking is provided by private owners and operators and that the free hour ended in October 2026 [3].

Fines are 60 euros in Vantaa and 80 euros in downtown Tikkurila [4]. The city's traffic report says about 44,700 parking violations were recorded in 2025, the highest in the series [5], and that fees paid for street parking were 258,000 euros in 2025 against 284,000 in 2024, partly because up to about half of the paid spaces in Tikkurila's 2-euro zone were removed in autumn 2025 for construction [6]. Kuusijärvi became a third payment zone in May 2025, with 390 spaces at 0.50 euro an hour [7].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The tram is the main change: a 19-km line from Mellunmäki via Tikkurila to the airport area with 27 stops, on which the first rails were laid on 11 May 2026, with 2029 given as the opening year [12]. Its works already cost spaces: the Ratatie P1 park-and-ride north of Tikkurila station closed in October 2025 to become a temporary bus terminal, while P3 stayed in use [13], and Tikkurila's park-and-ride transactions fell about 21 percent because tram works cut spaces [9]. Elsewhere, district parking in housing areas still being built in Kivistö, Keimolanmäki and Kaskela runs as a temporary solution, with about 150 monthly permits sold a month in 2025, 30 percent fewer than in 2024 [10][11]. Helsinki Airport has over 300 EV charging points at 0.25 euro per kWh [16].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
Park and ride is run by the city and feeds the national LIIPI service operated by Fintraffic [14]. The register shows 18 City of Vantaa park-and-ride car parks in operation with about 1,940 spaces, the largest being Härkälenkki P1 (496 spaces), Teatteripolku P3 (214) and Ratastie P1 (195) [15]. Autumn park-and-ride occupancy from hand counts was 45 percent in 2025, the same as in 2024 [8], with about 286,000 transactions in 2025, led by Kivistö with 84,000 [9]. At Helsinki Airport Finavia runs the parking, which can be pre-booked for 1 to 45 days [17].

Our data cover four of the city's park-and-rides with 975 spaces, measured since 27 September 2026. Occupancy averaged about 31% on weekdays and 29% at weekends, weighted by spaces, below the 45 percent the city's counts give. They differ widely: Kivistön asema P1 (114) averaged 72% and reached full on a Monday at about 10:00, Härkälenkki P1 (496) 31%, Ratastie P1 (195) 28% on weekdays but 10% at weekends, and Radioasemantie P2 (170) only 4%. About four weeks of data, taken before the end of the free first hour could show an effect.
